**Primary composite (CV death or HF hospitalization) in each trial:**

- **DAPA-HF** (HFrEF, LVEF ≤40%): 16.3% vs 21.2%, HR 0.74 (95% CI 0.65–0.85), P<0.001, over a median 18.2 months. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Reduced** (HFrEF): 19.4% vs 24.7%, HR 0.75 (0.65–0.86), P<0.001, median 16 months. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 361 of 1863 patients (19.4%) in the empagliflozin group and in 462 of 1867 patients (24.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.86; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Preserved** (HFpEF): 13.8% vs 17.1%, HR 0.79 (0.69–0.90), P<0.001, median 26.2 months; the effect was mainly related to lower HF hospitalization. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)"} -->
- **DELIVER** (HFmrEF/HFpEF): 16.4% vs 19.5%, HR 0.82 (0.73–0.92), P<0.001, median 2.3 years. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)"} -->

**Does the effect hold across the EF range?** Yes, as far as the sources state. In the meta-analysis of five trials (21,947 participants), SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the composite of CV death or HF hospitalization (HR 0.77, 0.72–0.82), with treatment effects for each endpoint consistently observed in the mildly reduced/preserved-EF trials and across all five trials; effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction."} --> In the two preserved-EF trials combined (12,251 participants), the composite was reduced by HR 0.80 (0.73–0.87), with consistent reductions in CV death (0.88, 0.77–1.00) and first HF hospitalization (0.74, 0.67–0.83). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87])"} --> DELIVER reported similar results in patients with LVEF ≥60% and <60%. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"Results were similar among patients with a left ventricular ejection fraction of 60% or more and those with a left ventricular ejection fraction of less than 60%"} -->

One caveat from the sources: the CV-death component alone was not significantly reduced in the preserved-EF trials (EMPEROR-Preserved's benefit was mainly fewer HF hospitalizations; DELIVER's CV death HR 0.88, 0.74–1.05).

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"with consistent reductions in both components: cardiovascular death (0·88 [0·77-1·00]) and first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·74 [0·67-0·83])"} -->

So: cardiovascular death was significantly reduced in the reduced-EF setting (DAPA-HF) and in the overall five-trial meta-analysis, but in the preserved/mildly reduced EF trials the effect was driven by hospitalization for heart failure, with CV death not reaching significance in DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved individually or in their pooled analysis.

**Reduction in all-cause mortality:** In the meta-analysis of five randomised heart failure trials (21,947 participants), SGLT2 inhibitors reduced all-cause mortality (HR 0·92, 95% CI 0·86–0·99), alongside reductions in cardiovascular death or HF hospitalisation (0·77 [0·72–0·82]), cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79–0·95]) and first HF hospitalisation (0·72 [0·67–0·78]).

**No significant difference:** In the empagliflozin chronic kidney disease trial, there were no significant between-group differences for death from any cause (4.5% empagliflozin vs 5.1% placebo), nor for the composite of HF hospitalisation or cardiovascular death (4.0% vs 4.6%) — although all-cause hospitalisation was lower with empagliflozin (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.78–0.95; P=0.003).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"there were no significant between-group differences with respect to the composite outcome of hospitalization for heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes (which occurred in 4.0% in the empagliflozin group and 4.6% in the placebo group) or death from any cause (in 4.5% and 5.1%, respectively)"} -->

answer:
**ARRIVE** (moderate-risk patients, diabetes excluded): aspirin did **not** significantly reduce events. The primary composite endpoint occurred in 269 (4.29%) aspirin vs 281 (4.48%) placebo patients (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038) over a median 60 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)"} -->

**ASCEND** (patients with diabetes, no evident cardiovascular disease): aspirin **did** significantly reduce serious vascular events, but bleeding offset this. Over a mean 7.4 years, serious vascular events occurred in 658 (8.5%) aspirin vs 743 (9.6%) placebo participants (rate ratio 0.88; 95% CI 0.79–0.97; P=0.01), while major bleeding occurred in 314 (4.1%) vs 245 (3.2%) (rate ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.09–1.52; P=0.003). The authors concluded the absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"The absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard."} -->

**ASPREE** (healthy older adults): aspirin did **not** significantly lower cardiovascular disease. Over a median 4.7 years, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 vs 11.3 events per 1000 person-years (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.83–1.08), while major hemorrhage was higher with aspirin (8.6 vs 6.2 events per 1000 person-years; HR 1.38; 95% CI 1.18–1.62; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08)"} -->

**JPPP** (Japanese patients aged 60–85 with atherosclerotic risk factors): no significant reduction. The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was 2.77% with aspirin vs 2.96% without (HR 0.94; 95% CI 0.77–1.15; P=.54).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54)."} -->

In short: only ASCEND showed a statistically significant cardiovascular reduction, and it was offset by major bleeding; ARRIVE, ASPREE and JPPP showed no significant cardiovascular benefit.

**2009 collaborative meta-analysis (Lancet, individual participant data; 6 primary-prevention trials, 95,000 individuals, 660,000 person-years)**

- Benefit: aspirin allocation gave a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% vs 0.57% per year, p=0.0001), driven mainly by about a fifth reduction in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.18% vs 0.23% per year, p<0.0001); the net effect on stroke was not significant (0.20% vs 0.21% per year, p=0.4), and vascular mortality did not differ (0.19% vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), due mainly to a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction"} -->
- Harm: major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds increased (0.10% vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001)"} -->
- Net balance: framed as uncertain — "aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds," with further trials in progress.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds."} -->

**2019 JAMA meta-analysis (13 trials, 164,225 participants, 1,050,511 participant-years; median baseline cardiovascular risk 9.2%)**

- Benefit: significant reduction in the composite cardiovascular outcome (57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 0.89, 95% credible interval 0.84–0.95; absolute risk reduction 0.38%, NNT 265).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"Aspirin use was associated with significant reductions in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 61.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265)."} -->
- Harm: increased major bleeding (23.1 vs 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 1.43, 95% credible interval 1.30–1.56; absolute risk increase 0.47%, NNH 210).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"Aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding events compared with no aspirin (23.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 16.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210)."} -->
- Net balance: framed as a trade-off rather than a verdict — aspirin was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding, information that "may inform discussions with patients."
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding."} -->

**Comparison:** The relative cardiovascular benefit is of similar magnitude (12% reduction in serious vascular events in 2009; HR 0.89 in 2019), but the 2019 analysis quantifies the absolute trade-off explicitly: the bleeding harm (absolute increase 0.47%, NNH 210) is larger in absolute terms than the cardiovascular benefit (absolute reduction 0.38%, NNT 265). The 2009 paper expressed the net effect as "uncertain" pending further trials; the 2019 paper, with the added trials, presents the same direction of effects and leaves the net balance to patient-level discussion rather than declaring net benefit.

This information may inform discussions with patients about aspirin for primary prevention"; it does not declare a net verdict, leaving the trade-off to patient discussion. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding."} -->

answer:
**Populations enrolled**

- **ARRIVE** (Lancet, 2018): 12,546 patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event, enrolled between July 5, 2007 and Nov 15, 2016 at 501 sites in seven countries; eligible patients were aged ≥55 years (men) or ≥60 years (women) with average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. Median follow-up was 60 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} -->

- **ASPREE** (NEJM, 2018): from 2010 through 2014, community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged ≥70 years (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the US) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability; participants received 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->

- **JPPP** (JAMA, 2014): 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, followed up to 6.5 years (last follow-up May 2012); open-label, randomized, parallel-group.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

**Relation to the USPSTF recommendations**

The USPSTF recommendation statement addresses adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual; the net benefit is small, and those not at increased bleeding risk willing to take it daily are more likely to benefit (C recommendation). The Task Force concludes with moderate certainty of a small net benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} -->

- **Ages 60 or older:** the USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention (D recommendation), concluding with moderate certainty of no net benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->

**How the evidence lines up:** the three trials enrolled almost entirely the age group the USPSTF now recommends against — ARRIVE's entry thresholds (men ≥55, women ≥60) and JPPP's 60–85 years fall at or above 60, and ASPREE enrolled ≥70 (≥65 for US blacks and Hispanics). Their populations were also largely free of established CVD, matching the recommendation's scope, but ARRIVE excluded diabetes and high-bleeding-risk patients, and ASPREE required freedom from CVD, dementia and disability — so these trials did not test the 40–59-year, ≥10% risk group for which the C recommendation applies.

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

answer:
**The three trials**

- **ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018): enrolled patients at *moderate* estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event — men aged 55 years and older and women aged 60 years and older, with average cardiovascular risk judged moderate by number of risk factors; patients at high bleeding risk or with diabetes were excluded. 12,546 patients were randomized (aspirin 6,270; placebo 6,276) at 501 sites in seven countries, median follow-up 60 months; the primary endpoint occurred in 4.29% vs 4.48% (HR 0.96, 95% CI 0.81–1.13).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} -->

- **ASPREE** (NEJM 2018): enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the US) who did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability; participants received 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo. Aspirin produced a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and no significantly lower cardiovascular disease risk than placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} -->

- **JPPP** (JAMA 2014): 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1,007 clinics in Japan (March 2005–June 2007), followed up to 6.5 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations (2022 statement)** — population: adults 40 years or older without signs, symptoms, or known CVD who are not at increased bleeding risk.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Ages 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk**: the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual; the net benefit is small (moderate certainty), and those not at increased bleeding risk who are willing to take it daily are more likely to benefit — a **C recommendation**.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Ages 60 or older**: the USPSTF recommends **against** initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention — a **D recommendation**; moderate certainty of no net benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->

**Relation to the trial evidence**: the trial populations sit largely in the ≥60 age band that the USPSTF recommends against. ASPREE (age ≥70, or ≥65 for US blacks/Hispanics) and JPPP (60–85 with atherosclerotic risk factors) both enrolled older adults, and ASPREE found more major hemorrhage with no cardiovascular benefit — consistent with a no-net-benefit conclusion in that group. ARRIVE's moderate-risk patients were somewhat younger (men ≥55, women ≥60) but excluded diabetes and high-bleeding-risk patients, and showed no significant reduction in the primary endpoint (HR 0.96), so it does not supply evidence of benefit for the 40–59 group's individualized decision either.

answer:
Here is how major bleeding compared with warfarin in the four pivotal trials:

**RE-LY (dabigatran)** — Major bleeding was 3.36%/year with warfarin vs 2.71%/year with dabigatran 110 mg (P=0.003, significantly lower) and 3.11%/year with dabigatran 150 mg (P=0.31, not significant). Hemorrhagic stroke was lower with both doses (0.12% and 0.10%/year vs 0.38%/year, P<0.001 for both).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 3.36% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 2.71% per year in the group receiving 110 mg of dabigatran (P=0.003) and 3.11% per year in the group receiving 150 mg of dabigatran (P=0.31)."} -->

**ROCKET AF (rivaroxaban)** — No significant between-group difference in major bleeding, though intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently with rivaroxaban.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8ff4bad2e9d926335b4de77ad1e41630","quote":"There was no significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding, although intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently in the rivaroxaban group."} -->

**ARISTOTLE (apixaban)** — Major bleeding was 2.13%/year with apixaban vs 3.09%/year with warfarin (HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.60–0.80; P<0.001), i.e. significantly less.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 2.13% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 3.09% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.80; P<0.001)"} -->

**ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (edoxaban)** — Major bleeding was 3.43%/year with warfarin vs 2.75%/year with high-dose edoxaban (HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.71–0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61%/year with low-dose edoxaban (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.41–0.55; P<0.001) — both significantly lower.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"The annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.43% with warfarin versus 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.71 to 0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001)."} -->

Summary: major bleeding was significantly lower than warfarin with dabigatran 110 mg, apixaban, and both edoxaban regimens; not significantly different with dabigatran 150 mg or rivaroxaban.

**The meta-analysis** (Lancet 2014, pooling all 71,683 participants of RE-LY, ROCKET AF, ARISTOTLE and ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 — 42,411 on a new oral anticoagulant, 29,272 on warfarin) concluded:

- **Stroke/systemic embolism:** reduced by 19% vs warfarin (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73–0·91; p<0·0001), **mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke** (0·49, 0·38–0·64; p<0·0001).
- **All-cause mortality:** reduced (0·90, 0·85–0·95; p=0·0003).
- **Intracranial haemorrhage:** reduced (0·48, 0·39–0·59; p<0·0001).
- **Gastrointestinal bleeding:** **increased** (1·25, 1·01–1·55; p=0·04).

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"New oral anticoagulants significantly reduced stroke or systemic embolic events by 19% compared with warfarin (RR 0·81, 95% CI 0·73-0·91; p<0·0001), mainly driven by a reduction in haemorrhagic stroke (0·49, 0·38-0·64; p<0·0001)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"New oral anticoagulants also significantly reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85-0·95; p=0·0003) and intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39-0·59; p<0·0001), but increased gastrointestinal bleeding (1·25, 1·01-1·55; p=0·04)."} -->

**Consistency with the individual trials:**

- **RE-LY** (dabigatran vs warfarin): haemorrhagic stroke 0·38%/year on warfarin vs 0·12%/year with 110 mg (P<0·001) and 0·10%/year with 150 mg (P<0·001) — a reduction of roughly 68–74%, consistent in direction and broadly in magnitude with the pooled ~51% reduction.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"The rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.38% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 0.12% per year with 110 mg of dabigatran (P<0.001) and 0.10% per year with 150 mg of dabigatran (P<0.001)."} -->

- **ARISTOTLE** (apixaban vs warfarin): haemorrhagic stroke 0·24%/year vs 0·47%/year (HR 0·51, 95% CI 0·35–0·75; P<0·001) — a 49% reduction, essentially identical to the pooled RR of 0·49.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of hemorrhagic stroke was 0.24% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 0.47% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.51; 95% CI, 0.35 to 0.75; P<0.001)"} -->

So yes — both trials individually reported significant reductions in haemorrhagic stroke versus warfarin, consistent with the meta-analysis's pooled finding.

**Low-dose edoxaban in ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48** (Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation): both once-daily regimens — including the low-dose one — were noninferior to warfarin for prevention of stroke or systemic embolism and were associated with significantly lower rates of bleeding and death from cardiovascular causes. The trial randomized 21,105 patients with moderate-to-high-risk AF, median follow-up 2.8 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"Both once-daily regimens of edoxaban were noninferior to warfarin with respect to the prevention of stroke or systemic embolism and were associated with significantly lower rates of bleeding and death from cardiovascular causes."} -->

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"Low-dose new oral anticoagulant regimens showed similar overall reductions in stroke or systemic embolic events to warfarin (1·03, 0·84-1·27; p=0·74), and a more favourable bleeding profile (0·65, 0·43-1·00; p=0·05), but significantly more ischaemic strokes (1·28, 1·02-1·60; p=0·045)."} -->

**15 mg edoxaban in ELDERCARE-AF** (Low-Dose Edoxaban in Very Elderly Patients with Atrial Fibrillation): in very elderly Japanese patients (≥80 years) with nonvalvular AF who were not appropriate candidates for standard-dose anticoagulation, once-daily edoxaban 15 mg was superior to placebo in preventing stroke or systemic embolism and did not produce a significantly higher incidence of major bleeding than placebo; 984 patients were randomized 1:1 (492 edoxaban, 492 placebo), and there was no substantial between-group difference in all-cause death (9.9% vs 10.2%; HR 0.97, 95% CI 0.69–1.36).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_0e9d75e95b4aa172897de8e3f4333228","quote":"In very elderly Japanese patients with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation who were not appropriate candidates for standard doses of oral anticoagulants, a once-daily 15-mg dose of edoxaban was superior to placebo in preventing stroke or systemic embolism and did not result in a significantly higher incidence of major bleeding than placebo."} -->

answer:
**Primary composite outcome (cardiovascular death or heart failure hospitalization) in each trial:**

- **DAPA-HF** (reduced EF): HR **0.74** (95% CI 0.65–0.85; P<0.001) — 16.3% vs 21.2% over a median 18.2 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Reduced** (reduced EF): HR **0.75** (95% CI 0.65–0.86; P<0.001) — 19.4% vs 24.7% over a median 16 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 361 of 1863 patients (19.4%) in the empagliflozin group and in 462 of 1867 patients (24.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.86; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Preserved** (EF >40%): HR **0.79** (95% CI 0.69–0.90; P<0.001) — 13.8% vs 17.1% over a median 26.2 months, mainly driven by lower hospitalization for heart failure.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)"} -->
- **DELIVER** (mildly reduced or preserved EF): HR **0.82** (95% CI 0.73–0.92; P<0.001) — 16.4% vs 19.5% over a median 2.3 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)"} -->

**Does the effect hold across the EF range?** Yes. Pooling DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved (12,251 participants), the composite was reduced with HR 0.80 (95% CI 0.73–0.87), with consistent reductions in both components — cardiovascular death 0.88 (0.77–1.00) and first HF hospitalization 0.74 (0.67–0.83).

Across all five trials (21,947 participants), the composite fell with HR 0.77 (0.72–0.82), and treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of composite cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure (0·77 [0·72-0·82])"} -->

answer:
## Cardiovascular death alone vs. hospitalization for heart failure

**The short answer:** In the individual trials, the benefit on the composite was driven mainly by hospitalization for heart failure; cardiovascular death alone was not significantly reduced in any single trial. Only when pooled did the meta-analysis show a modest, nominally significant reduction in cardiovascular death.

### DAPA-HF (reduced ejection fraction)
The primary outcome was a composite of worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death; the conclusion states the risk of "worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower" with dapagliflozin, regardless of diabetes status. The knowledge base does not contain a separate hazard ratio for cardiovascular death alone in DAPA-HF.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"Among patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, the risk of worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes."} -->

### DELIVER (mildly reduced or preserved ejection fraction)
Composite primary outcome: HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.73–0.92; P<0.001). Worsening heart failure: HR 0.79 (0.69–0.91). **Cardiovascular death alone: HR 0.88 (95% CI 0.74–1.05)** — i.e., not statistically significant.

**Populations**

- **CREDENCE** (Canagliflozin and Renal Outcomes in Type 2 Diabetes and Nephropathy): all patients had **type 2 diabetes** and albuminuric chronic kidney disease; entry required eGFR **30 to <90** ml/min/1.73 m² and albuminuria (albumin-to-creatinine ratio **>300 to 5000** mg/g), on renin-angiotensin system blockade; 4401 patients were randomized.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"we assigned patients with type 2 diabetes and albuminuric chronic kidney disease to receive canagliflozin, an oral SGLT2 inhibitor, at a dose of 100 mg daily or placebo. All the patients had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 30 to <90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and albuminuria (ratio of albumin [mg] to creatinine [g], >300 to 5000)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"4401 patients had undergone randomization, with a median follow-up of 2.62 years"} -->

- **DAPA-CKD** (Dapagliflozin in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease): 4304 participants with eGFR **25 to 75** ml/min/1.73 m² and urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio **200 to 5000** mg/g; the trial was explicitly designed to include patients **with or without type 2 diabetes**.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"We randomly assigned 4304 participants with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 25 to 75 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area and a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of 200 to 5000"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effect of dapagliflozin in patients with chronic kidney disease, with or without type 2 diabetes, is not known."} -->

- **EMPA-KIDNEY** (Empagliflozin in Patients with Chronic Kidney Disease): the broadest entry — eGFR **≥20 to <45** ml/min/1.73 m², **or** eGFR **≥45 to <90** with albumin-to-creatinine ratio **≥200** mg/g; described as "a wide range of patients with chronic kidney disease."
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"we enrolled patients with chronic kidney disease who had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of at least 20 but less than 45 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, or who had an eGFR of at least 45 but less than 90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 with a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of at least 200"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Among a wide range of patients with chronic kidney disease who were at risk for disease progression"} -->

So: CREDENCE was the narrowest (diabetes mandatory, lowest eGFR bound 30, albuminuria >300); DAPA-CKD was intermediate (eGFR 25–75, ACR 200–5000, diabetes optional); EMPA-KIDNEY was the broadest (eGFR down to 20, or higher eGFR with ACR ≥200).

**Consistency with and without diabetes**

- CREDENCE enrolled only patients with type 2 diabetes, so no diabetes-free comparison exists; its benefit was shown in that population (primary outcome hazard ratio 0.70; 95% CI 0.59 to 0.82; P = 0.00001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"The relative risk of the primary outcome was 30% lower in the canagliflozin group than in the placebo group"} -->
- DAPA-CKD: effects were similar in participants with and without type 2 diabetes, and the benefit was seen regardless of diabetes status.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effects of dapagliflozin were similar in participants with type 2 diabetes and in those without type 2 diabetes."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes, the risk of a composite of a sustained decline in the estimated GFR of at least 50%, end-stage kidney disease, or death from renal or cardiovascular causes was significantly lower with dapagliflozin than with placebo"} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY: results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across eGFR subgroups.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges."} -->

The knowledge base does not state the exact proportions of patients with and without diabetes in DAPA-CKD or EMPA-KIDNEY.

None of the four trials showed a statistically significant reduction in cardiovascular events.

**ARRIVE** (moderate-risk patients, 12,546 randomized, median 60 months): the primary composite endpoint occurred in 269 (4.29%) on aspirin vs 281 (4.48%) on placebo — HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038. Not significant.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)"} -->

**ASCEND** (diabetes, no evident cardiovascular disease): aspirin *did* prevent serious vascular events, but the absolute benefit was largely counterbalanced by major bleeding — the trial's own conclusion. Its conclusion states aspirin use prevented serious vascular events, though the absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events. The absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard."} -->

**ASPREE** (healthy elderly, 19,114 participants, median 4.7 years): cardiovascular disease rate 10.7 vs 11.3 events per 1000 person-years (HR 0.95; 95% CI 0.83–1.08) — not significantly lower than placebo, while major hemorrhage was higher (8.6 vs 6.2 per 1000 person-years; HR 1.38; 95% CI 1.18–1.62; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} -->

**JPPP** (Japanese patients 60–85 with atherosclerotic risk factors, N=14,464; terminated early for futility after median 5.02 years): 5-year cumulative primary outcome 2.77% (95% CI 2.40–3.20%) with aspirin vs 2.96% (2.58–3.40%) without — HR 0.94 (95% CI 0.77–1.15); P=.54. Not significant.

answer:
**Enrolled populations**

- **ARRIVE** — randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study in seven countries; eligible patients were men aged 55 years or older and women 60 years or older with average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, or with diabetes, were excluded. 12,546 patients were enrolled (aspirin n=6270, placebo n=6276) at 501 sites, median follow-up 60 months.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites."} -->

- **ASPREE** — community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States enrolled from 2010 through 2014, aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) without cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability; randomised to 100 mg enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability."} -->

- **JPPP** — multicentre, open-label, randomised, parallel-group trial; 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan (March 2005–June 2007), followed up to 6.5 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations and the evidence**

The recommendation applies to adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **Aged 40–59 with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk:** decision to initiate low-dose aspirin should be individual; net benefit is small (C recommendation). Moderate certainty.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->
- **Aged 60 or older:** USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation); no net benefit, moderate certainty.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

Relation to the trials: the three trials differ in population and design — moderate-risk adults (ARRIVE), older adults (ASPREE), and older Japanese adults with atherosclerotic risk factors (JPPP) — yet share a consistent direction of findings, a modest reduction in cardiovascular events with an increase in major bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54)."} -->

The 60-or-older recommendation rests on trials whose participants were mostly 60 or older — ASPREE (≥70, or ≥65 for blacks and Hispanics) and JPPP (60–85) — which showed no significant cardiovascular benefit and more major bleeding; ARRIVE, which enrolled men ≥55 and women ≥60, likewise found no significant reduction in its primary endpoint (4.29% vs 4.48%; HR 0.96).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)." -->

**Superior to warfarin on stroke or systemic embolism:**
- **RE-LY** — dabigatran 150 mg twice daily: 1.11%/yr vs 1.69%/yr with warfarin (RR 0.66; 95% CI 0.53–0.82; P<0.001 for superiority). The 110 mg dose was only non-inferior (1.53%/yr; RR 0.91; 95% CI 0.74–1.11; P<0.001 for non-inferiority).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"1.11% per year in the group that received 150 mg of dabigatran (relative risk, 0.66; 95% CI, 0.53 to 0.82; P<0.001 for superiority)"} -->
- **ARISTOTLE** — apixaban: 1.27%/yr vs 1.60%/yr (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.66–0.95; P<0.001 for non-inferiority; P=0.01 for superiority).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of the primary outcome was 1.27% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 1.60% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio with apixaban, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.66 to 0.95; P<0.001 for noninferiority; P=0.01 for superiority)."} -->

- **ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48** — both once-daily edoxaban regimens were "noninferior to warfarin with respect to the prevention of stroke or systemic embolism," with lower bleeding and cardiovascular death.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"Both once-daily regimens of edoxaban were noninferior to warfarin with respect to the prevention of stroke or systemic embolism"} -->

Major bleeding versus warfarin in the four pivotal trials:

**RE-LY (dabigatran, *Dabigatran versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation*)**: warfarin 3.36%/yr; dabigatran 110 mg 2.71%/yr (P=0.003, significantly lower); dabigatran 150 mg 3.11%/yr (P=0.31, not significantly different).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8a669b066c4cb002e5224ef48c9a8550","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 3.36% per year in the warfarin group, as compared with 2.71% per year in the group receiving 110 mg of dabigatran (P=0.003) and 3.11% per year in the group receiving 150 mg of dabigatran (P=0.31)."} -->

**ROCKET AF (rivaroxaban, *Rivaroxaban versus warfarin in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation*)**: no significant between-group difference in major bleeding, though intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less often with rivaroxaban.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8ff4bad2e9d926335b4de77ad1e41630","quote":"There was no significant between-group difference in the risk of major bleeding, although intracranial and fatal bleeding occurred less frequently in the rivaroxaban group."} -->

**ARISTOTLE (apixaban, *Apixaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation*)**: apixaban 2.13%/yr vs warfarin 3.09%/yr (HR 0.69; 95% CI 0.60–0.80; P<0.001) — significantly less major bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_81e343c146c92d15d7c2f15b65748ce1","quote":"The rate of major bleeding was 2.13% per year in the apixaban group, as compared with 3.09% per year in the warfarin group (hazard ratio, 0.69; 95% CI, 0.60 to 0.80; P<0.001)"} -->

**ENGAGE AF-TIMI 48 (edoxaban, *Edoxaban versus warfarin in patients with atrial fibrillation*)**: warfarin 3.43%/yr; high-dose edoxaban 2.75%/yr (HR 0.80; 95% CI 0.71–0.91; P<0.001); low-dose edoxaban 1.61%/yr (HR 0.47; 95% CI 0.41–0.55; P<0.001) — both doses significantly lower.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_1bcbd58b429315ec591b7e167517461a","quote":"The annualized rate of major bleeding was 3.43% with warfarin versus 2.75% with high-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.71 to 0.91; P<0.001) and 1.61% with low-dose edoxaban (hazard ratio, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.41 to 0.55; P<0.001)."} -->

- all-cause mortality: RR 0·90 (0·85–0·95; p=0·0003) <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"New oral anticoagulants also significantly reduced all-cause mortality (0·90, 0·85-0·95; p=0·0003)"} -->
- intracranial haemorrhage: RR 0·48 (0·39–0·59; p<0·0001) <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_68f0cec57cbc9a18bfbd4cfce07d3b63","quote":"and intracranial haemorrhage (0·48, 0·39-0·59; p<0·0001)"} -->

- **EMPEROR-Reduced** (HFrEF): HR 0.75 (95% CI 0.65–0.86, P<0.001); 19.4% vs 24.7% over a median 16 months. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_b5b2f2860d0e0ed2b6663cb104221791","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 361 of 1863 patients (19.4%) in the empagliflozin group and in 462 of 1867 patients (24.7%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio for cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure, 0.75; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.86; P<0.001)"} -->
- **EMPEROR-Preserved** (HFpEF): HR 0.79 (95% CI 0.69–0.90, P<0.001); 13.8% vs 17.1% over a median 26.2 months, driven mainly by lower HF hospitalization. <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)"} -->
- **DELIVER** (HFmrEF/HFpEF): HR 0.82 (95% CI 0.73–0.92, P<0.001); 16.4% vs 19.5% over a median 2.3 years; worsening HF HR 0.79 (0.69–0.91), CV death HR 0.88 (0.74–1.05). <!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)"} -->

**Across the ejection fraction range:** yes — the benefit is consistent. answer:
**Short answer: in the individual HF trials the primary benefit was driven mainly by hospitalization for heart failure; cardiovascular death alone was not clearly reduced in the HFmrEF/HFpEF trials, and only in the pooled five-trial meta-analysis did cardiovascular death reach significance.**

**DAPA-HF (HFrEF, EF ≤40%, n=4744):** the primary outcome was a composite of worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death, and it was reduced (16.3% vs 21.2%; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.85; P<0.001) over a median of 18.2 months. The trial conclusion states the risk of "worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes" was lower with dapagliflozin, regardless of diabetes — i.e. reported as the composite, not cardiovascular death on its own.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"Over a median of 18.2 months, the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"Among patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, the risk of worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes."} -->

**DELIVER (EF >40%, n=6263):** primary outcome, a composite of worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death, occurred in 16.4% vs 19.5% (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.73–0.92; P<0.001) over a median of 2.3 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"Over a median of 2.3 years, the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)."} -->

**EMPEROR-Preserved (EF >40%, n=5988):** primary outcome was the composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure; the conclusion is that empagliflozin reduced the combined risk, regardless of diabetes — again no separate claim for cardiovascular death alone.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"Empagliflozin reduced the combined risk of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure in patients with heart failure and a preserved ejection fraction, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes."} -->

**Meta-analysis (five trials, 21 947 participants):** the composite fell (0.77 [0.72–0.82]), first hospitalization for heart failure fell more sharply (0.72 [0.67–0.78]), and cardiovascular death alone was reduced (0.87 [0.79–0.95]), as was all-cause mortality (0.92 [0.86–0.99]).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"In the broader context of the five trials of 21 947 participants, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of composite cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure (0·77 [0·72-0·82]), cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79-0·95]), first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67-0·78]), and all-cause mortality (0·92 [0·86-0·99])."} -->

**In the HFmrEF/HFpEF subset (DELIVER + EMPEROR-Preserved, 12 251 participants):** the composite was reduced (0.80 [0.73–0.87]) with "consistent reductions in both components," but the cardiovascular-death component was borderline — 0.88 (0.77–1.00), touching 1.00 — whereas first hospitalization was 0.74 (0.67–0.83).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87]) with consistent reductions in both components: cardiovascular death (0·88 [0·77-1·00]) and first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·74 [0·67-0·83])."} -->

So: the reduction is consistently larger and more certain for hospitalization for heart failure than for cardiovascular death; cardiovascular death alone is statistically clear only in the pooled five-trial analysis, and is borderline in the preserved-EF pair. answer:
**Short answer: in the individual HF trials the primary benefit was driven mainly by hospitalization for heart failure; cardiovascular death alone was not clearly reduced in the HFmrEF/HFpEF trials, and only in the pooled five-trial meta-analysis did cardiovascular death reach significance.**

**DAPA-HF (HFrEF, EF ≤40%, n=4744):** the primary outcome was a composite of worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death, and it was reduced (16.3% vs 21.2%; HR 0.74, 95% CI 0.65–0.85; P<0.001) over a median of 18.2 months. The trial conclusion states the risk of "worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes" was lower with dapagliflozin, regardless of diabetes — i.e. reported as the composite, not cardiovascular death on its own.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"Over a median of 18.2 months, the primary outcome occurred in 386 of 2373 patients (16.3%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 502 of 2371 patients (21.2%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.74; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.65 to 0.85; P<0.001)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_3d8122c20e1cbc078636f036dbe476b7","quote":"Among patients with heart failure and a reduced ejection fraction, the risk of worsening heart failure or death from cardiovascular causes was lower among those who received dapagliflozin than among those who received placebo, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes."} -->

**DELIVER (EF >40%, n=6263):** primary outcome, a composite of worsening heart failure or cardiovascular death, occurred in 16.4% vs 19.5% (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.73–0.92; P<0.001) over a median of 2.3 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e1fc1fa13a9a3fbf27de970c81e78bba","quote":"Over a median of 2.3 years, the primary outcome occurred in 512 of 3131 patients (16.4%) in the dapagliflozin group and in 610 of 3132 patients (19.5%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.82; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.73 to 0.92; P<0.001)."} -->

**EMPEROR-Preserved (EF >40%, n=5988):** primary outcome was the composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure; the conclusion is that empagliflozin reduced the combined risk, regardless of diabetes — again no separate claim for cardiovascular death alone.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"Empagliflozin reduced the combined risk of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure in patients with heart failure and a preserved ejection fraction, regardless of the presence or absence of diabetes."} -->

**Meta-analysis (five trials, 21 947 participants):** the composite fell (0.77 [0.72–0.82]), first hospitalization for heart failure fell more sharply (0.72 [0.67–0.78]), and cardiovascular death alone was reduced (0.87 [0.79–0.95]), as was all-cause mortality (0.92 [0.86–0.99]).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"In the broader context of the five trials of 21 947 participants, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced the risk of composite cardiovascular death or hospitalisation for heart failure (0·77 [0·72-0·82]), cardiovascular death (0·87 [0·79-0·95]), first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·72 [0·67-0·78]), and all-cause mortality (0·92 [0·86-0·99])."} -->

**In the HFmrEF/HFpEF subset (DELIVER + EMPEROR-Preserved, 12 251 participants):** the composite was reduced (0.80 [0.73–0.87]) with "consistent reductions in both components," but the cardiovascular-death component was borderline — 0.88 (0.77–1.00), touching 1.00 — whereas first hospitalization was 0.74 (0.67–0.83).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Among 12 251 participants from DELIVER and EMPEROR-Preserved, SGLT2 inhibitors reduced composite cardiovascular death or first hospitalisation for heart failure (hazard ratio 0·80 [95% CI 0·73-0·87]) with consistent reductions in both components: cardiovascular death (0·88 [0·77-1·00]) and first hospitalisation for heart failure (0·74 [0·67-0·83])."} -->

So: the reduction is consistently larger and more certain for hospitalization for heart failure than for cardiovascular death; cardiovascular death alone is statistically clear only in the pooled five-trial analysis, and is borderline in the preserved-EF pair. Note also that treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4b1be72f0031135f81e0915e571e919b","quote":"Treatment effects on the primary endpoint were generally consistent across the 14 subgroups examined, including ejection fraction."} -->

- **DAPA-CKD** (dapagliflozin): 4304 participants with eGFR 25 to 75 ml/min/1.73 m² and a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 200 to 5000; enrolled with or without type 2 diabetes.

<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effect of dapagliflozin in patients with chronic kidney disease, with or without type 2 diabetes, is not known."} -->
- **EMPA-KIDNEY** (empagliflozin): eGFR ≥20 to <45, or eGFR ≥45 to <90 with a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of at least 200 — i.e., the broadest entry, including patients with little or no albuminuria.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"We enrolled patients with chronic kidney disease who had an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of at least 20 but less than 45 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 of body-surface area, or who had an eGFR of at least 45 but less than 90 ml per minute per 1.73 m2 with a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio (with albumin measured in milligrams and creatinine measured in grams) of at least 200."} -->

So: CREDENCE required diabetes and the heaviest albuminuria; DAPA-CKD required albuminuria but not diabetes; EMPA-KIDNEY allowed a wider eGFR range, including lower albuminuria, and did not require diabetes.

- DAPA-CKD: effects were similar in participants with and without type 2 diabetes.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_01c40038ab279aadbaf12401aadbad29","quote":"The effects of dapagliflozin were similar in participants with type 2 diabetes and in those without type 2 diabetes."} -->
- EMPA-KIDNEY: results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_9babb063478831150659a9e2e6b0e443","quote":"Results were consistent among patients with or without diabetes and across subgroups defined according to eGFR ranges."} -->
- CREDENCE: the knowledge base gives no with/without-diabetes comparison, since all its patients had type 2 diabetes; its result was a 30% lower relative risk of the primary composite (HR 0.70; 95% CI 0.59–0.82).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_57ce472296b677f0d08707b04c50a8f0","quote":"The relative risk of the primary outcome was 30% lower in the canagliflozin group than in the placebo group, with event rates of 43.2 and 61.2 per 1000 patient-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.59 to 0.82; P = 0.00001)."} -->

**EMPEROR-Preserved** (Empagliflozin in Heart Failure with a Preserved Ejection Fraction, NEJM 2021; NCT03057951):

- **5988 patients** were randomly assigned — those with class II–IV heart failure and an ejection fraction of **more than 40%** — to empagliflozin 10 mg once daily or placebo, in addition to usual therapy; the primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death or hospitalization for heart failure.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"we randomly assigned 5988 patients with class II-IV heart failure and an ejection fraction of more than 40% to receive empagliflozin (10 mg once daily) or placebo, in addition to usual therapy"} -->

- Over a median of 26.2 months, a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) on empagliflozin vs. 511 of 2991 (17.1%) on placebo (HR 0.79; 95% CI 0.69–0.90; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_343c67f35a2bf841907858fd63302653","quote":"Over a median of 26.2 months, a primary outcome event occurred in 415 of 2997 patients (13.8%) in the empagliflozin group and in 511 of 2991 patients (17.1%) in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.79; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.69 to 0.90; P<0.001)"} -->

For contrast, the companion trial in reduced EF (EMPEROR-Reduced) randomized 3730 patients with EF ≤40%.

**No — in none of the four trials did aspirin produce a statistically significant reduction in cardiovascular events; only ASCEND showed a significant (modest) reduction.**

- **ARRIVE** (moderate-risk patients, 12,546 randomized, median 60 months): primary composite endpoint (cardiovascular death, MI, unstable angina, stroke, TIA) in 269 (4.29%) on aspirin vs 281 (4.48%) on placebo — HR 0.96 (95% CI 0.81–1.13; p=0.6038), not significant.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038)"} -->
- **ASCEND** (15,480 patients with diabetes, mean 7.4 years): serious vascular events in 658 (8.5%) vs 743 (9.6%) — rate ratio 0.88 (95% CI 0.79–0.97; P=0.01), a significant reduction; major bleeding 4.1% vs 3.2% (rate ratio 1.29; 95% CI 1.09–1.52; P=0.003), so benefits were "largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard."
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01)"} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_98e15daeb7feed7b008fd69ffce6745f","quote":"The absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard."} -->
- **ASPREE** (19,114 older adults, median 4.7 years): cardiovascular disease 10.7 vs 11.3 events per 1000 person-years — HR 0.95 (95% CI 0.83–1.08), not significant; major hemorrhage 8.6 vs 6.2 per 1000 person-years, HR 1.38 (95% CI 1.18–1.62; P<0.001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08)"} -->

- **JPPP** (14,464 Japanese patients aged 60–85 with atherosclerotic risk factors, open-label, up to 6.5 years): 5-year cumulative primary outcome 2.77% (95% CI 2.40–3.20) with aspirin vs 2.96% (95% CI 2.58–3.40) without — HR 0.94 (95% CI 0.77–1.15; P=.54), not significant.

answer:
## Cardiovascular benefit

**2009 (Lancet collaborative meta-analysis):** In the primary prevention trials, aspirin produced a **12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events** (0.51% vs 0.57% per year, p=0.0001), driven mainly by a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.18% vs 0.23% per year, p<0.0001); the net effect on stroke was not significant (0.20% vs 0.21% per year, p=0.4).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"In the primary prevention trials, aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), due mainly to a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.18%vs 0.23% per year, p<0.0001)."} -->

**2019 (JAMA):** Across 13 trials (164,225 participants), aspirin was associated with a significant reduction in the composite cardiovascular outcome (57.1 vs 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 0.89, 95% credible interval 0.84–0.95; absolute risk reduction 0.38%, 95% CI 0.20%–0.55%; number needed to treat 265).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"Aspirin use was associated with significant reductions in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 61.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265)."} -->

So the proportional benefit is closely similar — a 12% reduction in serious vascular events in 2009 versus an 11% reduction (HR 0.89) in 2019.

## Bleeding harm

**2009:** Aspirin increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10% vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001), and the main risk factors for coronary disease were also risk factors for bleeding."} -->

**2019:** Major bleeding was increased (23.1 vs 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years; HR 1.43, 95% credible interval 1.30–1.56; absolute risk increase 0.47%, 95% CI 0.34%–0.62%; number needed to harm 210).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"Aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding events compared with no aspirin (23.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 16.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210)."} -->

Here the harm appears larger in 2019: the relative increase in major bleeding is 43% versus the 2009 excess expressed only as an absolute difference (0.10% vs 0.07% per year).

## Framing of net balance

**2009** framed primary prevention as of **uncertain net value**: "the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds," with further trials in progress.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8d9ae273169bf27b347ca66421434090","quote":"In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds."} -->

**2019** framed it as a trade-off to be discussed with patients rather than a verdict: aspirin was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding, and "this information may inform discussions with patients about aspirin for primary prevention."
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_64f23983bfe8fd167aa6725f288d7375","quote":"The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding."} -->

Note the difference in emphasis: 2009 explicitly labels net value "uncertain," whereas the 2019 conclusion reports both associations without declaring a net verdict. The two also differ in method — individual participant data from six primary prevention trials (95,000 individuals) in 2009 versus a systematic review of 13 trials using Bayesian and frequentist meta-analysis in 2019.

**Populations enrolled**

- **ARRIVE** (Lancet 2018, *Use of aspirin to reduce risk of initial vascular events in patients at moderate risk of cardiovascular disease (ARRIVE)*): men aged 55 years and older and women aged 60 years and older with average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate based on the number of specific risk factors; patients at high risk of gastrointestinal or other bleeding, and patients with diabetes, were excluded.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_a80cd40ea6db9ff8486b4ad6e10638d2","quote":"Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors. We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes."} -->

- **ASPREE** (*Effect of Aspirin on Cardiovascular Events and Bleeding in the Healthy Elderly*): community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States aged 70 years or older (or ≥65 years among blacks and Hispanics in the US) without cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability; 19,114 enrolled, median 4.7 years follow-up.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_e9c7fb4c1ac80a88d29e42eb4e27608e","quote":"Of the 19,114 persons who were enrolled in the trial, 9525 were assigned to receive aspirin and 9589 to receive placebo."} -->

- **JPPP** (Japanese Primary Prevention Project): 14,464 patients aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus, recruited at 1007 clinics in Japan, followed up to 6.5 years.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_8c085ce86e8550efe8d1ab710dba800f","quote":"Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, and were followed up for up to 6.5 years"} -->

**USPSTF recommendations (2022 statement) and the evidence**

- Population covered: adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding"} -->

- **40–59 years with ≥10% 10-year CVD risk**: individual decision; small net benefit (moderate certainty), C recommendation; those not at increased bleeding risk and willing to take daily low-dose aspirin are more likely to benefit.
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one."} -->

- **60 years or older**: recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin (D recommendation); no net benefit (moderate certainty).
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation)."} -->
<!-- evimed-source:{"sourceId":"src_4634e2a7a07fd8375f49298d2fb101f7","quote":"The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit."} -->

**Relation to the trials**: the three trials sit largely at or above the 60-year threshold where the USPSTF recommends against initiation — ASPREE enrolled only persons 65/70 and older, and JPPP only ages 60–85, so both fall squarely in the D-recommendation group; ARRIVE's entry ages (men ≥55, women ≥60) straddle the boundary, with the women from 60 onward in the D group and the men aged 55–59 potentially in the 40–59 individualized-decision group. The knowledge base does not state the USPSTF's own explicit trial-by-trial linkage to ARRIVE, ASPREE, or JPPP.
